content: Haff disease is a condition characterized by the rapid onset of rhabdomyolysis, which involves the swelling and breakdown of skeletal muscle tissue. This condition carries a risk of acute kidney failure and typically develops within 24 hours of consuming fish. The first documented case of Haff disease occurred in 1924 near Königsberg on the Baltic coast, in individuals residing around the Haff region, which is how the disease got its name. Between 1925 and 1940, approximately 1,000 cases were reported, not only in humans but also in birds and cats. These cases were linked to the consumption of fish such as burbot, eel, and pike. In the United States, only 26 cases were reported between 1984 and 2014. As living standards improve and fish consumption increases, the number of cases has also risen. Haff disease is a rare clinical syndrome with an unclear pathophysiology. It has been suggested that palytoxin, a heat-stable toxin with thiaminase activity, may play a role in its development. This toxin cannot be inactivated by cooking due to its heat-stable nature. The exact cause of Haff disease remains unknown, and further research is needed to clarify its etiology. Haff disease causes rhabdomyolysis and must be distinguished from other causes of rhabdomyolysis. These causes can be categorized into physical, non-physical, and genetic factors. Physical factors include trauma, excessive muscular activity, status epilepticus, high-grade fever, heatstroke, and electric shock. Non-physical factors include medications, infections, drugs, and electrolyte abnormalities. Genetic factors include autoimmune diseases, metabolic disorders, and various inherited conditions. Haff disease has been reported worldwide, but the specific fish species associated with the condition vary by geographic location. In Eastern Europe and Sweden, burbot, pike, freshwater eel, and whitefish are the primary culprits. In China, freshwater pomfret and crayfish have been implicated, while in Japan, boxfish has been associated with the disease. In the United States, buffalo fish, crayfish, and Atlantic salmon have been linked to cases. The incubation period for Haff disease is approximately eight hours. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, muscle rigidity, chest pain, sweating, and brown-colored urine (myoglobinuria). Although the condition is generally self-limiting with a good prognosis, complications such as acute kidney injury and disseminated intravascular coagulation can occur in some cases. Symptoms of Haff disease typically develop within 24 hours of consuming cooked seafood. These symptoms include nausea, vomiting, muscle pain (myalgia), muscle rigidity, chest pain, sweating, shortness of breath (dyspnea), and brown urine. On physical examination, findings may include muscle tenderness, weakness, and myoglobinuria. The diagnostic criteria for Haff disease include a history of consuming cooked seafood within 24 hours prior to symptom onset, elevated serum creatine phosphokinase (CPK) levels, and a CK-MB fraction of less than 5%. Laboratory evaluation should include a complete blood count (CBC), creatine kinase levels, serum electrolytes, liver function tests, urine pH, and urinalysis. Haff disease may lead to cardiac arrhythmias due to hyperkalemia and hypocalcemia, which result from rhabdomyolysis. Therefore, it is essential to monitor the patient with an electrocardiogram (ECG). Ultrasound imaging may reveal hypoechoic areas in the muscles due to inflammation and fluid infiltration. Additional diagnostic studies are not typically required for the diagnosis of Haff disease. The treatment of Haff disease primarily involves medical management. This includes aggressive fluid hydration to address rhabdomyolysis, correction of electrolyte abnormalities such as hyperkalemia and hypocalcemia, and other supportive care measures. There is no surgical treatment indicated for Haff disease. Primary prevention of Haff disease involves avoiding the consumption of seafood species that have been associated with the condition.
